note:
Survey of free-to-use picture sources for Carolina barbecue and for pig art. Yields marked MEASURED were retrieved on this machine on 2026-09-16; yields marked REPORTED were verified by a research pass that loaded the pages but whose files this project has not downloaded. loc.gov, si.edu and collection.si.edu are all behind Cloudflare and refused every request from this machine; nypl.org is behind Imperva and dp.la behind AWS WAF. The subject splits in two: generic pig imagery is abundant and free, Carolina barbecue imagery is scarce and mostly encumbered.

SECOND PASS, 2026-09-16 (same day, later). validate.py's allowlist now accepts "No known copyright restrictions", NoC-US and "United States Government Work" alongside CC0 / public domain / CC BY / CC BY-SA / FAL, which opened the seam the first pass could see and could not take. Two harvesters were written: tools/harvest_flickr.py (Flickr, no API key, working from the public pages) and tools/harvest_archives.py (DigitalNC and CONTENTdm). 33 pictures were taken onto 24 records, 66 MB. By holder: State Archives of North Carolina 18, Southern Foodways Alliance 6, Edgecombe County Memorial Library 3, UNC-Chapel Hill 2, Nathan Cardozo 2, Joe Shlabotnik 1, Greenville County Library System 1. By statement: no known copyright restrictions 18, CC BY 2.0 7, public domain 3, NoC-US 3, CC BY-SA 2.0 2. Records that had no picture and now have one: scotts-famous-barbecue, adam-scott, parkers-barbecue, clyde-coopers, lexington-barbecue, bar-b-q-center, sweatmans-bar-b-que, bs-barbecue (two more), direct-heat, barbecue-chicken, and the term records barbecue, pit, hog and down-east. Still with no picture and no free candidate found anywhere: skylight-inn, stameys-barbecue, meltons-barbecue, bums-restaurant, gradys-barbecue, short-sugars, and hog-killing — every photograph of those is all rights reserved, and the refusals are itemised below.

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons
sources.what_it_holds: The only source that produced a picture for this project. Three strands. (1) Library of Congress mirrors: the John Margolies Roadside America archive, 11,710 slides of American signs and roadside buildings, 1969-2008; Carol M. Highsmith's America; the Farm Security Administration / Office of War Information negatives including Marion Post Wolcott's 1939 Carolina work. (2) Boston Public Library's Tichnor Brothers postcard collection, around 25,000 linen-era cards, 1930-1945, split by state. (3) Individual uploads: Dennis Brown's thirteen Pigs in the City sculptures at Lexington, Jay Cuthrell's Wilber's pig weather vane, Southern Foodways Alliance festival photographs, the City of Greenville's B's Barbecue set.
sources.licence_terms: Per file, stated on the file page and returned by the API as extmetadata.LicenseShortName. The harvester accepts CC0, Public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA and FAL and skips the rest. Margolies is public domain because the Library of Congress bought the intellectual property with the archive.
sources.how_to_fetch: tools/harvest_commons.py --search and --walk write triage to data/images/_triage/; --harvest <id> --apply downloads at 1200px with a JSON sidecar. No key. Two harvester faults found and fixed on 2026-09-16: the Library of Congress sets are uploaded as TIFF and Commons serves a JPEG rendition, which the tool was rejecting on the original's mime type, losing 463 triage rows including the whole Margolies corpus; and long titles truncated to the same 60 characters, so two files silently overwrote each other and a record claimed a checksum for bytes it did not have.
sources.yield: MEASURED. 196 queries, 7,363 rows, 7,233 free, 3,124 of them free raster images rather than scanned book pages. 115 pictures now on 22 records, 49 MB.
picks: File:Pig neon sign, Beale Street, Memphis, Tennessee LCCN2010630376.tif — Highsmith; a neon pig in sunglasses eating a pork sandwich under PORK WITH AN ATTITUDE!, the clearest example of the genre found anywhere

File:Bessinger's Bar-B-Q sign, West Columbia, South Carolina LCCN2017709630.tif — Margolies 1988; the pig Little Joe over BAR-B-Q, the best-documented Carolina pig sign
File:Steve's Bar-B-Q sign, Spencer, North Carolina LCCN2017709851.tif — Margolies 1982; a Pepsi-Cola cap in neon above the restaurant's own name

sources.name: State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons
sources.what_it_holds: 117,159 photographs. THE BEST SOURCE FOUND for actual Carolina barbecue: postcards of named joints from the PhC.184 Massengill Postcard Collection, Albert Barden's Raleigh negatives, John Hemmer's 1944 plantation barbecue, and pit-cooking photographs. This is where the Carolina roadside material lives, and it is in neither Commons nor Openverse.
sources.licence_terms: Flickr licence 7, 'No known copyright restrictions', which is NOT a public-domain declaration: the institution says it has found no copyright, shares that research without warranty, and asks the user to make an independent assessment before a new use. ⚠ THE STATEMENT IS PER PHOTOGRAPH, NOT PER COLLECTION, and this pass measured the split rather than assuming it. Of 616 photographs surveyed across the account, 96 were all rights reserved. The 2008-era uploads are the reserved ones and the 2015-onward re-uploads are the released ones, and the same negative appears both ways: the 2008 upload of N.53.17 314 is reserved, the two 2017 re-uploads are Commons — and those two are mirror images of each other, so the negative's orientation is not settled by this source either. The rule that follows is simple and was enforced in code: read the photograph's own page, every time.
sources.how_to_fetch: NOW HARVESTABLE. tools/harvest_flickr.py, stdlib only, no API key. A photo page states its rights three times — a numeric licence id in the page's photo model, the words in the title attribute of the <a rel="license">, and a licence URL on that anchor and again in the JSON-LD ImageObject — and prints every rendition's URL and width; the tool requires all three readings to name the same licence before it downloads a byte. That check earned its keep on the first run: Flickr now prints 'CC BY 2.0' and 'Public Domain Work' where the tool expected 'Attribution' and 'Public Domain Mark', and it refused twelve free photographs rather than guess. Searching: https://www.flickr.com/search/?user_id=24231108%40N08&text=<term>, and search barbecue and barbeque separately, they return different sets. ⚠ ONLY PAGE 1 IS SERVER-RENDERED — page 2 comes back with no results in the HTML — so 25 rows is the ceiling per query and coverage comes from many queries and from &sort=date-posted-desc and &sort=interestingness-desc, which reorder the same pool. A listing page carries each result's licence too, which is good enough to triage from and never good enough to download from.
sources.yield: MEASURED. 616 photographs surveyed over about 140 queries; 520 carrying licence 7. 18 taken. The account's barbecue seam is a handful of named collections, not a long tail: the Department of Conservation and Development News Bureau sheets (John Hemmer and Bill Sharpe, 1939-1951), the Albert Barden negatives, the PhC.184 Massengill postcards, the H. H. Brimley agriculture folders and the PhC.23 FCX street views.

The account holds no released hog-killing photograph; the pit/hog-killing record still leans on Tennessee and Virginia through Commons

NOT TAKEN though released: the Albert Barden company barbecues — Southern Bell Telephone 1940, 1941 and 1944, Motor Bearings and Parts 1941 and 1942, NC Equipment Co 1946 — are group portraits in a pine grove with no pit, no food and sixty identifiable faces, so they earn no place; N_53_15_6505, where the caption puts Sealey's Barbecue at 322 South Blount Street, but the sign cannot be read in the frame

sources.name: Flickr Commons — the other participating institutions
sources.what_it_holds: The first pass looked only at the State Archives. Two more Flickr Commons members hold Carolina barbecue material. UNC Libraries Commons has the North Carolina Postcards under the Public Domain Mark — the same cards UNC's own dcr.lib.unc.edu serves with no rights URI at all — including The Original Lexington Barbecue, Parker's Bar-B-Q, Rose's Village Motel with its VILLAGE BARBECUE sign, and the 1905-1915 Charlotte card overprinted 'Special North Carolina Barbecue'. The City of Greenville, North Carolina posts a set of about thirty-three B's Barbecue photographs under the Public Domain Mark; two of them already reached this project through Wikimedia Commons.
sources.licence_terms: Per photograph, stated on the photo page, and the tool reads it there. UNC's cards and Greenville's set are Flickr licence 10, the Public Domain Mark, which the page words as 'Public Domain Work'.
sources.how_to_fetch: tools/harvest_flickr.py --search "<term>" --user unclibraries_commons (or cityofgreenvillenc), then --harvest. Same 25-row page-1 ceiling as any Flickr search.
sources.yield: MEASURED. 3 pictures taken: the Lexington Barbecue postcard, the Charlotte 1905 postcard, and — through Commons earlier — the B's Barbecue frames. The UNC postcard seam is larger than the barbecue query finds, because a card's subject heading is often 'Restaurants' with no barbecue word anywhere in the metadata.
picks: The Original Lexington Barbecue -- North of Winston Salem, N.C. -- Hwy. 52 at Motor Rd. — https://www.flickr.com/photos/unclibraries_commons/22475472794/ — TAKEN
Charlotte, N.C. The Industrial Center of the New South, Special North Carolina Barbecue — https://www.flickr.com/photos/unclibraries_commons/22680294608/ — TAKEN

Parker's Bar-B-Q — https://www.flickr.com/photos/unclibraries_commons/22476297254/ — free, and the same photograph as the Massengill card already held, differently tinted; not taken to avoid a near-duplicate
Rose's Village Motel — https://www.flickr.com/photos/unclibraries_commons/22706355059/ — free, holds a VILLAGE BARBECUE sign; left for a later pass

sources.name: Southern Foodways Alliance on Flickr
sources.what_it_holds: Oral-history and Southern BBQ Trail photographs, including the working pits at Lexington Barbecue, B's Barbecue, Wilber's, Allen & Son, the Skylight Inn, Stamey's, Bum's, Short Sugar's, Grady's, Cook's, the Barbecue Center, Jack Cobb & Son, Bunn's, Sweatman's, Melvin's, Hite's and Brown's. It is the only place a photographer has gone into most of these pit rooms with a camera and put the results online.
sources.licence_terms: ⚠ THE ACCOUNT IS SPLIT BY PROJECT, NOT BY SUBJECT, and the split is the whole story. The 2007-2009 sets by Amy C. Evans and Alan Pike are CC BY 2.0. The 2012 North Carolina and South Carolina Barbecue Trail sets by Denny Culbert are ALL RIGHTS RESERVED — every frame. That is where the Skylight Inn, Stamey's, Bum's, Short Sugar's, Grady's, Cook's and the Barbecue Center live, which is why those records still have no picture. Nothing from the Culbert sets is used here.
sources.how_to_fetch: tools/harvest_flickr.py --search "<term>" --user southernfoodwaysalliance. The account's own description text carries the restaurant, the town, the photographer and the month, which is better metadata than most archives give.
sources.yield: MEASURED. 94 Carolina photographs surveyed, 22 of them CC BY 2.0 and the rest reserved. 6 taken.
picks: TAKEN — shoulders at Lexington BBQ, chopping shoulders at Lexington BBQ, bbq with slaw and hushpuppies at Lexington Barbecue, Amy C. Evans, February 2008 — the first pictures on the lexington-barbecue record
TAKEN — 09 Arthur House taking the first pig off of the pit, 02 B's Barbecue Rd. Sign, 10 Chickens on the pit, Alan Pike, July 2009

NOT TAKEN, free: Keith Allen with bbq chicken and pork at Allen & Son (allen-and-son already has two pictures); the B's plate, sauce, cabbage, potatoes, storefront and tobacco-field frames, eight more, all CC BY 2.0 and available

⛔ REFUSED, all rights reserved: the entire Skylight Inn set (about twenty-four frames, including James Howell salting the pigs on the pit and hands chopping pork on the block), the entire Stamey's set (about nineteen, including the pit house, the woodpile and coals going under the pit), Bum's whole hog on the pit, Grady's whole hog skin on the pit, Short Sugar's, Cook's, the Barbecue Center's red slaw, Jack Cobb & Son, Bunn's, Sweatman's pork ribs, Melvin's rotisserie, Brown's, Hite's

sources.name: Suicide Food (blog)
sources.what_it_holds: Not a picture source — the only systematic catalogue of the cannibal-pig genre anyone has made, and the thing that named it. 929 posts, 20 December 2006 to 27 December 2011, by a Seattle writer who signs himself Ben; the surname Grossblatt comes from Lindy West's profile in The Stranger on 1 November 2007 and appears nowhere in the blog's own text. Its definition is a depiction of animals that act as though they wish to be consumed. Every entry is rated on a five-point scale headed Psych Evaluations, counted in nooses. Tag counts: pig 539, bbq 399, chicken 238, cow 210, chef hat 114, sunglasses 107. An eleven-part series, 2007 to 2011, named the recycled stock pig logo Repetitious Porcine Emblemology. Still online; the last post calls the project a pause.
sources.licence_terms: All rights reserved, and its images are third-party advertising art. Citable and linkable, never harvestable.
sources.how_to_fetch: Read it. Blogger's JSON feed at /feeds/posts/summary?alt=json gives counts and tags. Archived at the Wayback Machine from 14 June 2007, roughly 410 snapshots.
sources.yield: Zero pictures, one whole record. Press: Cory Doctorow, Boing Boing, 19 April 2007; Lindy West, The Stranger, 1 November 2007; Andrew Simmons, LA Weekly, 7 July 2011; Mariann Sullivan, Our Hen House, 6 July 2011. Scholarship: none. OpenAlex returns three title-or-abstract hits and thirty-eight full-text hits for the phrase, all false positives. Carol J. Adams's anthropornography and Melanie Joy's carnism are real and citable, but nothing found connects either to the barbecue pig mascot, so this project does not.
picks: The header definition, for the one quotation the cannibal-pig-sign record uses
The noose scale, the genre's only published taxonomy
Repetitious Porcine Emblemology, a useful term with a citable origin
English Wikipedia's Suicide food article dates the term to the early 2010s, which the blog's own archive contradicts by four years; do not cite it for chronology

sources.name: DPLA — Digital Public Library of America
sources.what_it_holds: An index, not a holder: metadata plus a cached thumbnail, with every record pointing at the contributing institution. The facet that works is the hub, not the location: barbecue + partner="North Carolina Digital Heritage Center" returns 185, barbecue + partner="South Carolina Digital Library" returns 56. Note the naming is inverted from intuition — provider= returns nothing, partner= is the hub.
sources.licence_terms: Set by the contributor and frequently imprecise. Five rightsCategory values; only Unlimited Re-Use is safe, and it merges two unlike statements. NoC-US is a positive determination that the item IS public domain in the United States. NKC, No Known Copyright, is the absence of one: a conclusive determination could not be made. ⚠ The search-results payload STRIPS edmRights — never judge rights from a results page. Neither statement touches trademark, which is live here because a photograph of a branded barbecue sign can be copyright-free while the logo is not. ⚠ AND THE COUNT IS A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING. DPLA's rightsCategory facet counts only records carrying an edmRights URI. The North Carolina hub holds 291 records matching barbecue terms; 143 of them carry no edmRights at all, and among those are five UNC postcards whose holder's own rights field reads the bare words 'Public domain'. The first pass's 'nine freely reusable items' is the URI-bearing subset, and two of those nine are Duke broadsides about a Virginia and a Mississippi barbecue. The same artifact produced the first pass's 'ZERO open in South Carolina': all 147 SC matches lack an edmRights URI, yet Greenville County Library System's and USC's own rights fields say 'Public Domain' in words. Reading a rights value out of DPLA is not reading a rights value.
sources.how_to_fetch: ⚠ dp.la NOW RETURNS HTTP 403 with a 'Request Blocked — DPLA' page even to a full browser header set; it is no longer readable from this machine at all. The route that works is the keyless S3 bulk export the first pass identified: https://s3.amazonaws.com/dpla-provider-export/, latest 2026/09/, per-hub files 2026/09/digitalnc.jsonl/ (5 gzipped parts, about 208 MB) and 2026/09/scdl.jsonl/ (2 parts, about 77 MB). Stream them through gunzip and grep rather than saving them; edmRights survives intact. Then leave DPLA: every rights statement used here was read on the holding institution's own page. ⚠ lib.digitalnc.org is behind AWS WAF and answers an ordinary request with an empty HTTP 202 whatever the user agent; tools/harvest_archives.py takes an aws-waf-token cookie from a browser session, and says so and stops when it has none. CONTENTdm sites need nothing: <base>/digital/api/collections/<alias>/items/<id>/false returns every metadata field including Rights. UNC's dc.lib.unc.edu is retired and 301s to dcr.lib.unc.edu/record/<uuid>. NARA, loc.gov and si.edu were not retried.
sources.yield: MEASURED where the first pass was REPORTED. 291 NC records and 147 SC records pulled from the S3 hub files. NC edmRights split: none 143, CNE 62, InC 59, NoC-US 9, UND 7, InC-EDU 6, NKC 2, PDM 1, InC-NC 1, InC-RUU 1. 4 items taken, each verified on its holder's page: three 1898 Tarboro photographs from the Edgecombe County Memorial Library and the one open South Carolina barbecue photograph, at Greenville.
picks: TAKEN — N.C. Barbecue, Pigs and Roast Pig, Tarboro, 1898, by Lena Pennington Martin — lib.digitalnc.org/record/242383, /242366, /242419 — rights field reads http://rightsstatements.org/vocab/NoC-US/1.0/. A shallow trench of coals with split pigs laid along it, a canvas awning down one side, men working it with long-handled tools. The library's description says 'possibly for the Democratic party mass meeting of October 18, 1898'; that hedge is carried into the records rather than firmed up

TAKEN — Annual Barbecue, circa 1950s, Union Bleachery employees at Paris Mountain State Park — cdm17168.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p17168coll61/id/45 — Rights field reads exactly 'Public Domain'. A serving line, women in aprons ladling from buckets, the queue winding back among the trees. Still the only openly licensed South Carolina barbecue photograph found. ⚠ Greenville's site prints a blanket infringement disclaimer above every record; that is site furniture, and the item's own Rights field is what was read

TAKEN, but through Flickr rather than DPLA — the UNC postcards. UNC's own repository states the rights only as the free-text words 'Public Domain' in a metadata field, with no URI anywhere in the record JSON; the same cards on UNC Libraries Commons carry the Public Domain Mark. The Flickr copies were taken because the statement there is the firmer one. The Original Lexington Barbecue (1930-1945) and Charlotte, N.C. ... Special North Carolina Barbecue (1905-1915) are now on records

MISSED BY THE FIRST PASS, free, not yet taken: Parker's Bar-B-Q (UNC, near-identical to the Massengill card already held, so it would duplicate) and Rose's Village Motel (UNC, ca. 1940-1960, whose lower right corner holds a large VILLAGE BARBECUE sign with CURB SERVICE and PLATE LUNCHES boards — a genuine candidate for the roadside-signs record, left for a later pass)

SEEN, FREE, DELIBERATELY NOT TAKEN: 'No Negro Officers' (lib.digitalnc.org/record/242265, NoC-US) — the fourth photograph in the same 1898 Tarboro series, an elevated view of a crowd under a white-supremacy campaign banner. The library cross-references it to the two pit photographs. It is not a barbecue picture and does not belong on a food page as decoration; a record that carries it would have to be about the 1898 campaign and would have to be written, not illustrated. Also not taken: Wright's Auto Machine Company BBQ, Durham, April 1943 (record/251599, NoC-US) — a panoramic group portrait of several hundred faces with no barbecue in the frame; Wilson County Civil War Veterans, 1903 (record/464, NoC-US) — the reunion included a barbecue dinner, none of it visible, and the file is JP2; Caddell's Cafe, Sanford (UNC, public domain) and Twin Lakes, Columbia (Richland Library, Public Domain) — the word barbecue is in the card text, not the picture

SEEN, FREE, NOT PICTURES: an 1825 invitation to a militia barbecue, Williams-Chesnut-Manning Family Papers, South Caroliniana Library, rights 'Public Domain' (digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/collection/wcmanning/id/1562); a programme for the Confederate veterans' re-union at Charlotte, 25 August 1909, Duke, 'Free Re-Use / No Copyright - United States', whose schedule reads '1:30 P. M.—Barbecue, at Latta Park' (idn.duke.edu/ark:/87924/r4x060n3p). Both are citable documents for a later pass

⛔ OFF LIMITS, rights read: Hagans Barbecue 1939 (InC); Wilber's Barbecue 1960 postcard (copyright status unknown); Sign for Piggie Park Bar-B-Q 1974, Richland Library (© The State Media Company, all rights reserved); about eleven Duke ROAD outdoor-advertising items including Randy's Circle-R Barbecue and Gompers Bar-B-Que Karnival, whose rights field says in words that the majority of the collection is not in the public domain; Carolina News and Guide at Furman, 'The rights status of this object is unclear and requires further research'

⛔ NOT TAKEN on judgement: the Official South Carolina BBQ trail map, 2022, SC State Library (dc.statelibrary.sc.gov/handle/10827/50646). Its rights note applies the government-edicts holding in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org — a case about annotations to a legal code — to a tourism brochure. That is the holder's determination, it is not a settled reading, the brochure is current rather than historical, and it is full of live restaurant marks
⛔ OUTSIDE CAROLINA: two of the nine NoC-US items are Duke broadsides for an 1860 Virginia barbecue and an 1844 Natchez, Mississippi one. Free, and not this subject

sources.name: Internet Archive
sources.what_it_holds: The best source for pig ENGRAVINGS — breed books and hog trade catalogues — and nothing at all for Carolina roadside. The Gilbert seed and nursery collection's identifier is usda-nurseryandseedcatalog, 93,315 items, 36,627 of them pre-1929.
sources.licence_terms: Per item, and all hedged. The Archive itself says it does not guarantee the copyright status of anything. Three per-item forms seen: possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; 'The Library of Congress is unaware of any copyright restrictions for this item'; 'The contributing institution believes that this item is not in copyright.' All three are beliefs. The sounder basis is the project's own test: a United States work published before 1 January 1930 is public domain by term expiry.
sources.how_to_fetch: advancedsearch.php with output=json; item metadata at /metadata/<id>; no key, no documented limit. IIIF works: manifest at https://iiif.archive.org/iiif/<id>/manifest.json, image at /iiif/<id>$<page>/full/max/0/default.jpg, ImageService3 level 2. The manifests carry no rights field — rights come only from the metadata API.
sources.yield: REPORTED. barbecue + texts + pre-1929 = 18 items, mostly political-rally speeches and newspaper pages, with NO barbecue plates. swine + texts + pre-1929 = 1,541. Gilbert crossed with swine or hog or Berkshire or Poland-China = 12, six of them pre-1929. "trade card" AND pig = ZERO, so the trade-card angle is not here. Commons already mirrors much of this: 3,687 of this project's 7,363 Commons triage rows were Internet Archive book scans, filtered out as page images rather than pictures.
picks: Harris on the pig: breeding, rearing, management, and improvement, 1870, 264 pp — https://archive.org/details/harrisonpigbreed01harr — the classic illustrated breed book
The hog: a treatise on the breeds, management, feeding and medical treatment of swine, Youatt 1855 — https://archive.org/details/hogtreatiseonbre00youarich — NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT
Hog raising in the South, S. M. Tracy, USDA 1899 — https://archive.org/details/CAT87201513
Full blood Poland china hogs, Clinton Falls Nursery Co., 1913 — https://archive.org/details/CAT31293713 — Gilbert collection
A barbecue toast, A. M. Ballard, Asheville N.C., 1900 — https://archive.org/details/barbecuetoast00ball — the only pre-1929 Carolina barbecue item on the Archive; text, not pictures

sources.name: New York Public Library Digital Collections
sources.what_it_holds: Thin for this subject, with one exception. barbecue returns 71 items, 66 public domain, but the 66 are largely a mirage: eight to ten are 1939-40 World's Fair microform index cards with no imagery at all, and about twenty-one are Farm Security Administration photographs of Colorado and Montana. barbecue + "North Carolina" returns 6. barbecue + "South Carolina" returns ZERO. ⚠ Period material under this heading is substantially racist caricature — minstrel sheet music with blackface covers — and the library flags it as such.
sources.licence_terms: Per item. The public-domain items say the library believes the item is in the public domain under United States law but made no determination for other countries, and ask for the credit 'From The New York Public Library' with a link back. The library's About page addresses the distinction directly: unless you are a lawyer or outside the United States, it says, there is not really a difference between public domain and no known U.S. copyright restrictions. Quote what each item page shows.
sources.how_to_fetch: The public-domain filter is literally &filters=%5Brights%3DpublicDomain%5D. ⚠ The site is behind Imperva; curl gets a 212-byte stub. But iiif.nypl.org, images.nypl.org and api.repo.nypl.org are NOT walled: https://iiif.nypl.org/iiif/3/<imageID>/full/max/0/default.jpg works keyless, and the image IDs are printed on each item page. ⚠ THE API IS DEPRECATED AND THE DATE HAS PASSED — api.repo.nypl.org says it will no longer be available from 1 August 2026, six weeks ago, with no replacement planned. It still answers 401 rather than 410. Do not build on it. The bulk repo at github.com/NYPL-publicdomain/data-and-utilities is archived read-only and its README says the data is a snapshot from 30 December 2015.
sources.yield: REPORTED. About nine usable Carolina images in total, plus the Green Book.

sources.name: The Negro Motorist Green Book (NYPL, Schomburg Center)
sources.what_it_holds: 23 items. Years digitised: 1937-1941, 1947-1957 including a 1949 Vacation Guide and a 1951 Railroad Edition, 1959-1963/64, and 1966-67. Missing: 1936, 1942-46, 1958, 1965. For the resources page, as the brief asked.
sources.licence_terms: NOT UNIFORM. Twenty-two of the twenty-three carry the library's public-domain belief statement. The 1966-67 International Edition does not: it carries an orphan-works statement — the item may be protected, no rights-holder has been identified or located — which is rightsstatements.org InC-RUU. Treat that volume as in copyright but unlocatable, not as free.
sources.how_to_fetch: Item pages; images through iiif.nypl.org keyless.
sources.yield: ⚠ CAROLINA LISTINGS ARE NOT FINDABLE BY SEARCH. The scans have no OCR. Verified by controlled test: a phrase that sits in the title metadata returns hits, while phrases from inside the pages return zero. The 1949 edition is 80 pages with no search-inside and no transcription. Finding a Carolina barbecue listing means paging through scans by eye. The Green Book data projects are dead: navigatingthegreenbook.org does not resolve, NYPL Labs's extraction was never finished, and github.com/NYPL/greenbook-data is 404. No downloadable dataset of listings exists.

sources.name: Smithsonian Open Access
sources.what_it_holds: Thin for this subject, and the pig mass is guinea pigs, wart-hogs, Hog Island and Porky Pig. Counts before throttling: pig 7,906 records / 2,312 with images; hog 4,170 / 2,465; barbecue 169 / 48; swine 190 / 30.
sources.licence_terms: ⚠ NOT QUOTABLE FROM HERE. si.edu, collection.si.edu, americanhistory.si.edu and ids.si.edu all return Cloudflare 403, the same block as loc.gov, so the terms of use and Open Access FAQ could not be read and are not paraphrased. What the data shows: CC0 is a machine-readable flag at content.descriptiveNonRepeating.online_media.media[].usage.access, and it sits on the MEDIA, not the record — a record with no media has no CC0 status at all.
sources.how_to_fetch: api.si.edu/openaccess/api/v1.0/search?q=&api_key= with a key from api.data.gov; filter syntax is Solr-ish, e.g. barbecue AND online_media_type:"Images". DEMO_KEY is capped at 30 requests an hour and 50 a day and was exhausted in minutes. The keyless route is the bulk metadata on S3: https://smithsonian-open-access.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/metadata/edan/index.txt, 37 unit indexes of line-delimited JSON.
sources.yield: REPORTED, and low. Of 15,421 National Museum of American History records parsed from the bulk data, only 167 had any online media at all. Five title matches for pig, hog, pork or barbecue, and every one had online_media null. Stream-grepping 64 of 256 NMAH chunks for CC0 media plus a pig or barbecue term gave zero. The 48 barbecue-with-images from the API are real but could not be seen. Worth one targeted pass with a real key, not a pipeline.

sources.name: South Carolina Digital Library, and UNC
sources.what_it_holds: ⚠ THE OLD SC DOMAINS ARE DEAD: scmemory.org and scdl.sc.edu do not resolve. The live aggregator is scmemory-search.org, a Blacklight instance over 40-odd institutions and more than 200,000 items, with a keyless JSON API at /catalog.json?q=barbecue (69 results). USC's own CONTENTdm is keyless too: digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/api/search/searchterm/barbecue — barbecue 132, pig 317, hog 369. UNC's current system is dcr.lib.unc.edu, with a keyless API at /api/searchJson?anywhere=barbecue returning 752; the old dc.lib.unc.edu CONTENTdm URLs that DPLA still cites now redirect there.
sources.licence_terms: Bad in South Carolina and absent at UNC. Richland Library's State Newspaper Photograph Archive — where most SC barbecue photography lives, including Maurice Bessinger with barbecue sandwiches, 1986 — is entirely 'Copyright © The State Media Company. All rights reserved.' ⚠ UNC's DCR EXPOSES NO RIGHTS STATEMENT AT ALL: a walk of the full record JSON for any key containing right, licen, copyr or permis returns only access flags. The 'Public domain' string DPLA shows for UNC postcards comes from legacy CONTENTdm metadata and is reproduced nowhere in UNC's current system. Documenting the American South is worse: its copyright page is a 404 and its permissions page carries no reuse statement. ⚠ UNC's missing rights statement has a way around it that the first pass did not find: the same postcards sit on UNC Libraries Commons on Flickr under the Public Domain Mark, which is a rights URI where the repository gives only free text. Where a holder publishes the same object twice, take the copy with the firmer statement.
sources.how_to_fetch: Keyless JSON at all three, as above. DigitalNC's own site is bot-walled (202 with an empty body) and has no JSON search, though OAI-PMH works at lib.digitalnc.org/oai2d; take DigitalNC through the DPLA S3 hub file instead.
sources.yield: REPORTED. Exactly one open South Carolina barbecue item found in the whole state aggregation. CORRECTED: the Greenville item IS in DPLA (dp.la/item/eae18667c3d9ba5f9949a4f205e8a0b6); the first pass said it was outside. It has now been taken, through the holder's own CONTENTdm API, whose Rights field reads 'Public Domain'. USC's South Caroliniana Library also has an 1825 militia-barbecue invitation marked 'Public Domain' in words. So the state's open count is not one item but at least two, and the first pass's 'ZERO' came from reading DPLA's facet instead of the holders' fields.

Wilber's Barbecue, North Carolina Postcards — https://dcr.lib.unc.edu/record/3f4fae2a-76bd-4e73-ac34-9533d5519b50 — no rights statement anywhere in UNC's system
Barbecue Lodge Restaurant, 4600 N. Blvd, Raleigh — https://dcr.lib.unc.edu/record/92f66231-5188-481a-ad7c-45dcda552bca — same

sources.name: Openverse, Pixabay, Unsplash
sources.what_it_holds: Near-useless for historic Carolina material, and one of them should be avoided outright.
sources.licence_terms: Openverse indexes only real licences and HAS NO nkc VALUE — ?license=nkc returns 400, so Flickr Commons material, including the State Archives stream above, is not in Openverse at all. It cannot find the best source. Pixabay is not CC0: its licence forbids selling or distributing content on a standalone basis, forbids commercial use of content containing recognisable trademarks — live here, since barbecue signage is full of brand marks — and forbids use as part of a trade mark. Unsplash is not CC0 either, and one clause should stop this project using it: the licence does not include the right to compile images from Unsplash to replicate a similar or competing service, which is arguably what a reference picture library is.
sources.how_to_fetch: Openverse: anonymous, no key, 20 requests a minute and 200 a day. ⚠ Its anonymous result_count is CAPPED AT 240 — every broad query returns exactly 240, so do not read that as a count; narrow queries are honest.
sources.yield: REPORTED. Real public-domain-mark or CC0 hits for "barbecue sign": 22, of which the named examples are Cincinnati and Omaha. Nothing Carolinian. Recommendation: use Openverse as a cross-index only, treat Pixabay as a last resort with a trademark check, and keep Unsplash out of a compiled picture library entirely.

sources.name: Library of Congress (loc.gov), NARA, and the American Sign Museum
sources.what_it_holds: Three that could not be exercised. loc.gov holds the originals of the three collections that carried this project and almost certainly holds Carolina pig signs that never reached Commons — the Margolies collection code is mrg. NARA's catalogue was unreachable too. The American Sign Museum in Cincinnati, founded 1999 by Tod Swormstedt whose family published Signs of the Times, open since 2005 and in a former parachute factory in Camp Washington since June 2012, has more than 3,800 items catalogued and around 200 on display — the one institution that collects this object as an object.
sources.licence_terms: loc.gov: no known restrictions on publication for Margolies, Highsmith and FSA/OWI alike; Margolies is public domain because the Library bought the intellectual property. NARA: federal records, but its API terms forbid scraping and direct bulk users to the AWS open-data registry. The Sign Museum's own photographs are its own.
sources.how_to_fetch: loc.gov is BLOCKED: HTTP 403 to every request from this machine, browser user agent included, and to the JSON API and photos search alike. Use the Commons mirrors and search by the photographer's name. NARA needs a key and returns the single-page-app HTML shell to every unauthenticated path, so 'wrong path' and 'auth gate' cannot be told apart from here; its limit is 10,000 queries a month by default.
sources.yield: NOTHING DIRECTLY. Everything credited to the Library of Congress in this project came through Commons. The largest known unexplored seam is a browser search of the mrg collection for barbecue and pig, which a person can do and this machine cannot.
